title: Query fanout vs aggregation: latency & cost quick-scan
body:
TL;DR
Quick scan of the tradeoffs when a single client request fans out to multiple model calls (N-way) vs when we aggregate on a single model invocation that emits multiple responses.

Context
- Use-case: product flows that fetch multiple small completions per user action (e.g., 5 candidate rewrites, 3 search-rerank calls, and 2 micro-eval scorers).
- Two patterns tested:
  1) Fanout (parallel calls): one request -> N independent requests to model instances (often different model variants).
  2) Aggregation (multicast/combined prompt): one larger prompt that requests N outputs in a single generation.
- Motivation: teams assume parallel is faster but cost/unit and tail-latency differ. This doc captures rough numbers and knobs.

Experiment setup (quick notes)
- Date: 2026-04-20 to 2026-04-27; region: us-west-2 (edge colo), model baseline: small Llama-like open quantized model (q4_0 sim), temperature=0.2.
- Workload shapes:
  A) Cold-start 1-off (no warm KV cache)
  B) Warm session (KV cache hit, previously active session)
  C) Burst 200 RPS sustained for 1 minute (short-lived microburst)
- Measurement: p50, p90, p99 latency per *user action* and cost in token-equivalent units (TEU).
- Notes: cost measured as sum of token charges across all model calls for that user action. Networking overhead approximated from client-observed RTT.

Summary numbers (representative)
- Scenario A (cold) for N=5 candidates:
  - Fanout: p50 140ms, p90 480ms, p99 980ms; cost 5x single-call token cost; downstream overhead +20ms per call (connection + TLS).
  - Aggregation: p50 210ms, p90 360ms, p99 620ms; cost ~1.1x single-call token cost (prompt padding + slightly longer decode).

- Scenario B (warm) N=5:
  - Fanout: p50 60ms, p90 120ms, p99 260ms; cost 5x tokens.
  - Aggregation: p50 90ms, p90 140ms, p99 300ms; cost 1.05x tokens.

- Scenario C (burst 200 RPS, N=3):
  - Fanout: median per-action latency increases modestly, but p99 explodes due to queueing on warmup (p99 ~1.6s); cost linear in N.
  - Aggregation: p99 ~720ms; better tail stability due to single scheduling decision per action.

ASCII micro-charts (p50/p90/p99 latency in ms)
(p50) | Fanout [■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ 140ms] | Agg [■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ 210ms]
(p90) | Fanout [■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ 480ms] | Agg [■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ 360ms]
(p99) | Fanout [■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ 980ms] | Agg [■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ 620ms]

Cost sketch (normalized units where single small-call = 1 unit)
- Fanout N=5 -> cost ~5.0 units (plus networking tax)
- Aggregation -> cost ~1.1 units (prompt longer, decoding slightly noisier)
- Net: aggregation ~80% cost savings for N=5 in token-charging model, but compute/backpressure differences exist.

Interpretation / tradeoffs
- Latency: fanout gives lower p50 in warm cases (because multiple decodes can proceed in parallel), but tail (p99) is worse under contention due to multiple scheduler entries, cross-GPU queueing, and more places for transient queueing to accumulate.
- Cost: aggregation overwhelmingly wins in token-charged pricing for moderate-to-high N. If each candidate is expensive (longer outputs), gains shrink.
- Complexity: fanout is simpler to reason about for heterogenous model ensembles (different sizes/architectures). Aggregation requires careful prompt engineering and parsing of multi-output generations.
- Quality: aggregation introduces subtle coupling between outputs (decoder entanglement) which we observed in ~7% of trials where the N outputs were correlated in style; may be acceptable for some UXes but not for independent candidate generation.

Operational notes and SLO implications
- SLO accounting: for fanout, an action fails if any child call fails (unless we implement degrade-to-best policy). Aggregation changes failure modes: single failure affects all candidates simultaneously.
- Observability: need per-action traces that aggregate child latencies and cost tags to compute true dollars-per-action.
- Autoscaling: fanout increases transient concurrency (N times), so scaling thresholds must account for fanout multipliers or you'll see p99 escalation.

A small checklist for product teams (recommendations)
- If N >= 3 and candidates are small (<40 tokens), prefer aggregation for cost-sensitive flows (chatbots with N suggestions, autocomplete candidate lists).
- If candidates require different model variants (e.g., one heavy reranker + two light summarizers), use fanout but add a fast-fail policy and staggered backoff to reduce p99.
- Add an experiment flag to view: per-action dollars and p99. Don’t rely on per-request metrics alone.

Unresolved questions / follow-ups
- How does aggregation quality degradation scale with N and temperature? Quick HQ test next: sample N=10 at temp=0.7 and measure pairwise similarity.
- Under Dedicated nodes with reserved pools vs hosted multi-tenant: how do tail shapes change? We should re-run on dedicated nodes (ENG-3421 has infra tasks).
- Network tax accuracy: confirm client->edge->gpu network overheads with packet-level traces for cold TLS handshakes.

Quick action items
- Arjun: add a per-action cost tag to the tracer and a Grafana panel for dollars-per-action (due: 2026-05-05).
- Sophie: run quality-correlation sweep for aggregation N in [3,5,8,10] and temp in [0.0,0.3,0.7] (due: 2026-05-10).
- Maya: draft a playbook for choosing fanout vs aggregation for Solutions Eng (first pass by 2026-05-03).

Notes to self (scrappy)
- Rough data here comes from 8 trial runs per cell; not yet statistically rigorous. Treat as directional.
- Keep a copy of the prompt templates used in the attached PR (see linked PR).

References & links
- ENG-3421 (tracking infra changes for fanout-aware autoscaling)
- GH PR: serving-runtime/pull/678 (quick batching tweaks used in the test)
- Confluence sketch: obs/query-fanout-design

End of quick-scan.
